claims.text: Introducing a high density of deformation-induced nano-twins through controlled severe plastic deformation will improve the strength–plasticity balance of refractory high-entropy alloys.
A tailored severe plastic deformation protocol involving high-strain-rate deformation at cryogenic or room temperature can induce nano-twins throughout the microstructure.
The intervention will form a uniform intragranular distribution of nano-twins and a high density of twin boundaries.
Nano-twins and twin boundaries impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion caused by nano-twins increases strength.
Nano-twins provide additional mechanisms for plastic accommodation.
Plastic accommodation associated with nano-twins improves ductility.
The nano-twinned alloy will have a statistically significant increase in yield strength relative to the same alloy processed without significant nano-twin formation.
The yield-strength increase will occur without compromising plasticity.
The intervention may enhance ductility relative to the conventionally processed reference alloy.
The proposed effect requires alloy compositions and stacking-fault energies conducive to twinning.
The proposed improvement should hold when mechanical properties are tested at room or moderately elevated temperatures.
If an alloy's properties do not favor twinning, severe plastic deformation may not produce the predicted improvement.
Direct evidence for nano-twin-induced strength–plasticity optimization in refractory high-entropy alloys is limited.
Most supportive trends come from studies of non-refractory high-entropy alloy systems.

contradictions.description: The prediction permits unchanged plasticity as long as yield strength increases, whereas the falsification rule's phrase 'do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in yield strength and/or plasticity' can be read as requiring a significant plasticity increase. Thus, an outcome allowed by the prediction could be treated as falsifying under the stated rule.

The falsification rule requires both lack of property improvement and lack of increased nano-twin density. If nano-twin density increases but the strength–plasticity balance does not improve, the central causal hypothesis has failed, yet the stated conjunctive rule would not clearly classify it as falsified.
